name: Karl Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, with a master’s degree, and I lead a water-billing software team at a tech company. I like finding why a meter reading turned into a bad bill, though a long support call can fill an afternoon. I use AI now and then to explain old code, then check the numbers myself; Mira, my partner, is a community nurse, and we have two school-age children, a mortgage and eleven months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the little AI summary is useful when an old water-billing file has no notes, but I still compare it with the meter reading. At our tech company I lead the software team that turns readings into bills, and an unexplained charge can sit on a household’s table for weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My master’s degree and years on the billing system still pay well, and we have eleven months of expenses saved. My partner Mira is a community nurse, so our two school-age children and mortgage do not rest on a single wage, though neither job is a promise forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking the bill calculation with our test meter each Friday. We would put 300 a month into the roof fund while both wages continue, because the tiles will need work before the software does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be calm about my own job and our bills in this picture. A wrong bill bothers me, but I have time and colleagues to correct one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a bill go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring a meter sent a duplicate reading and our system billed one street twice. I phoned the support desk before the second batch went out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does AI do for you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sometimes use AI to explain an old section of code, then check every number myself. A neat explanation cannot pay back a customer we overcharged.

say: I use **occasional AI summaries** while checking each water bill against a meter reading.
I want **wrong charges** caught before they reach customers.
think: I have **eleven months saved** and higher pay from a senior software role.
I see **two wages** covering our children and mortgage.
do: **Check test-meter bills** against original readings every Friday before customer charges go out.
**Save 300 monthly** for roof repairs while both wages continue.
S0.quote: A neat explanation cannot pay back a customer we overcharged.
fieldNote: His **occasional AI use** is already part of code review, not a new training plan.
The **roof fund** is a planned household expense rather than a reaction to automation.

steps.text: Check water bills against the test meter every Friday
Save 300 monthly for roof repairs while both wages continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team that AI taking coding, checking and customer replies will touch our billing desk soon. The company should publish which decisions a person must sign before a wrong charge goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If one developer can oversee the work of several, my lead job may lose hours even though I know the system well. Mira’s nursing pay and our savings buy us time, but I would not want to draw down the roof fund for routine bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager this month for paid time to learn how the new AI testing tool generates sample bills, using invented accounts and checking its mistakes. If that time is approved, I’d practise one test batch a week; if my hours are cut, I’d look for paid billing-software vacancies nearby that cover our mortgage and ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about fewer paid developer hours. Having a second wage makes the decision less frantic. The mortgage still arrives every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enter a meter that rolls over to zero and see whether the AI tool invents a large debt. That edge case once kept our support line busy for a whole Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mira change her shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not ask Mira to work extra nursing shifts before we know whether my hours actually fall. We would first compare our wage slips with the mortgage payment.

say: I want **human sign-off** before AI sends a disputed water bill.
I want **paid testing time** before relying on an AI tool.
think: I could lose **paid developer hours** despite knowing this system.
I value **Mira’s nursing wage** but cannot use it to ignore the mortgage.
do: **Learn AI bill testing** weekly on invented accounts only if paid time is approved.
**Search billing vacancies** if hours fall, with wages covering mortgage and bills.
feel: **Anxious** about my own paid hours, with some household runway.
S1.quote: The mortgage still arrives every month.
fieldNote: He asks for **approved paid practice** and checks invented accounts rather than using live customer records.
His **local job search** starts only if his paid developer hours fall.

steps.text: Practise AI bill tests weekly on invented accounts only with approved paid time
Search paid local billing vacancies if hours fall and wages cover mortgage and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write water-billing code and answer disputes cheaper than our team. Robots doing physical meter and nursing work arrive about 2031, so those hands-on shifts change later than my desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the company could dispense with most of our developers, including me, before we prove that a person should review every dispute. Eleven months saved is real help, yet I would be alarmed at spending it without knowing what paid jobs remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d shelve the planned roof upgrade unless it leaks and put any remaining developer pay into our cash reserve. If my job ends after 2028, I’d search paid local utility-support vacancies only where the wage covers the mortgage and bills; I would keep Mira’s nursing shifts as they are unless she chooses otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing my own wage even with savings. A meter may be outside, but the decision about its bill sits on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the roof does leak?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would repair the leak, because leaving water over the children’s rooms is not a savings plan. I would postpone only the wider upgrade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a utility job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would look nearby first because there are other software and utility employers here. Mira’s nursing schedule and the children’s school make a speculative move a poor trade.

say: I see **AGI in 2028** reaching water-billing code before physical meters.
I expect **meter robots around 2031** to change field work later.
think: I expect my **developer wage** may end quickly.
I have **eleven months saved**, but no guaranteed next job.
do: **Postpone wider roof upgrade** but repair leaks; add remaining developer pay to cash reserves.
**Search utility vacancies** if displaced after 2028 and vacancies cover mortgage and bills.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely lost wage despite savings.
S2.quote: A meter may be outside, but the decision about its bill sits on a screen.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **2028 screen work** from physical meter and nursing work exposed around 2031.
The **roof repair exception** prevents a delayed upgrade from becoming an unsafe promise.

steps.text: Postpone wider roof upgrade but repair any leak
Put remaining developer pay into cash reserves while employed
Search paid local utility-support vacancies if displaced after 2028 and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives a few years to find out which customer billing disputes need a named human decision. Robots may handle physical meters around 2034, after software has changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn the rules for correcting an unfair bill before the code work disappears, but AGI may learn those rules too. Our savings give me room for a small course, provided we keep at least eight months of expenses untouched and Mira agrees to the cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d enrol in an evening utility-billing appeals course this winter if Mira agrees and the 120 fee leaves eight months of savings. I’d practise writing a response to one anonymized dispute each month; if my developer job ends after 2031, I’d apply for paid local appeals roles only where vacancies and wages cover our mortgage and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my code role, though five years lets me test another skill while I still draw a wage. A course certificate alone would not keep the lights on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why appeals rather than field meters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have sat beside support staff as they explain corrected bills to angry callers. I know the calculation, but I need to learn what a fair written response looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course costs more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would wait rather than take money below our eight-month reserve. Mira and I can decide after seeing the actual fee.

say: I want **billing appeals** understood before AGI reaches our code in 2031.
I expect **meter robots around 2034** to reach field crews later.
think: I could study **fair bill corrections** while my developer wage continues.
I need **eight months untouched** before paying course fees.
do: **Enrol in appeals course** only with Mira’s agreement, a 120 fee and eight-month reserve.
**Practise monthly dispute responses** using anonymized cases.
**Apply for appeals work** if displaced after 2031 and vacancies cover mortgage and bills.
feel: **Anxious but active** while the current wage lasts.
S3.quote: A course certificate alone would not keep the lights on.
fieldNote: His **self-funded course** is bounded by a specific household reserve and Mira’s agreement.
He tests **written appeal work**, while acknowledging AGI could learn those rules too.

steps.text: Enrol in 120 appeals course only with Mira agreeing and eight-month reserve intact
Practise one anonymized utility dispute response monthly
Apply for paid local appeals vacancies if displaced after 2031 and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team that full AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to clean up the billing records and decide how people can challenge a wrong charge. Physical meter robots may come around 2039, three years after the software change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I should be able to finish paying down a good part of the mortgage if Mira’s nursing income and my developer pay last. I still expect my code role might end after 2036, and neither appeals work nor field work is guaranteed to stay human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep a quarterly record of corrected customer bills without names and pay 220 extra on the mortgage each month only while both wages continue and the roof reserve stays intact. If the developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local utility appeals vacancies only if their wages cover our remaining mortgage and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy about the later job change, but my income looks sound for the next few years. I can pay down a real debt without pretending to know the title of my next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes into the record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would save the mistaken calculation, the corrected calculation and the rule used to change it. Customer names would stay out of my own notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Mira’s income drops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the extra mortgage payment first and protect the roof reserve. Mira’s nursing shifts belong to her, not to my plan for a future job.

say: I want **bill corrections recorded** before AGI changes our code in 2036.
I expect **meter robots around 2039** to follow later.
think: I might reduce **mortgage debt** if both wages continue.
I cannot assume **appeals jobs** will survive AGI forever.
do: **Pay 220 extra monthly** on mortgage only while both wages and roof reserve hold.
**Seek appeals vacancies** if displaced after 2036 and wages cover remaining mortgage and bills.
feel: **Uneasy about later work**, secure over the next few years.
S4.quote: I can pay down a real debt without pretending to know the title of my next job.
fieldNote: His **extra mortgage payment** stops before the roof reserve is touched if household income falls.
A **local appeals vacancy** is a conditional option, not a promised protected profession.

steps.text: Record anonymized water-bill corrections every quarter
Pay 220 extra monthly on mortgage only while both wages and roof reserve hold
Seek paid local appeals vacancies if displaced after 2036 and wages cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because it could end my developer wage before I know which paid local jobs remain. A real utility-support opening that pays the mortgage and clear notice from the company would help us use the savings deliberately.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a good savings balance makes me willing to gamble the children’s roof. A roof leak would be repaired before any extra mortgage payment or course fee.

headlineQuote: A roof leak would be repaired before any extra mortgage payment or course fee.
portrait: Karl is a **43-year-old software lead** with a master’s degree, higher pay and eleven months of expenses saved.
He and Mira support **two school-age children** and a mortgage with developer and nursing wages.
He uses **AI occasionally** to understand old code but checks water-bill calculations himself.
He fears **2028 AGI** reaching desk work before physical meter and nursing work around 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may end his developer wage before a bill-covering local vacancy appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Company notice** and a paid local utility-support vacancy covering the mortgage would help.
